findings.title: Payment processors prohibit 'fast, easy money' offers, which threatens how make-money-online coaching offers collect cash
findings.detail: Stripe's restricted-businesses list (updated 22 Sep 2026) prohibits get-rich-quick schemes, including sites that promise fast, easy money, and recruitment-based multi-level marketing (MLM). It restricts negative-option marketing and unclear trial pricing, and bans evading card-network chargeback monitoring. Business coaching and high-ticket coaching are not named specifically.
findings.why_it_matters: Growth operators often set up checkout, payment plans and financing for creator clients. Offer copy and refund handling directly affect the risk of a processor freezing funds. A pre-launch claims and policy review, plus refund and chargeback-rate monitoring, protects revenue that the rev share depends on.

findings.title: High-ticket sales funnel benchmarks: booking 40-50%, show 55-85%, close 12-40% depending on price, with cost-per-booked-call ceilings by tier
findings.detail: Inflo Partners (Sep 2026) gives these benchmarks for $5K+ offers: booking 40-50% of applications (35-40% with manual follow-up, 55-60% with instant booking links), show 75-85% (under 70% means weak pre-call nurture), and close 25-40% (executive coaching 45-50%). It recommends weekly team review, tracking by source and by rep, and judging trends over 4-6 weeks. It expects a close-rate dip for several weeks after a new rep starts. Its triage order is: booking below 35% means follow-up is broken; low show means fixing nurture with reminders at 48h, 24h and 2h; close below 20% means checking rep skill, fit and qualification. Leads Now AI (May 2026, vendor dataset it says covers 50,769+ booked calls) gives close from booked call of 12-38% and show of 55-80%. It puts premium offers ($30K+) at 12-15% close. Its profitable cost-per-booked-call ceilings are about $150-300 for $3-7K offers, $400-700 for $10-12K offers and $800-1,500 for $15-30K offers.
findings.why_it_matters: These are the default targets and alert thresholds for the KPI dashboard and the weekly review agent: booking, show and close rates by source and rep, plus cost per booked call against the price tier. The triage order can run as an automated diagnosis that a person approves before acting.

findings.title: Choosing a funnel: VSL for $5-12K offers and fast tests, webinar for higher ticket or warm audiences, application funnel at $15K+ with volume, and a VSL plus weekly webinar hybrid
findings.detail: Inflo (Jul 2026) maps funnels to price and stage. A VSL suits $5-12K offers: 2-4% of ad clicks book a call, setup takes 1-2 weeks, and it is good for testing positioning. A webinar suits higher-ticket offers: 8-15% of attendees book a call, and setup takes 2-3 weeks. An application funnel (8-12 questions, someone to review forms) suits $15K+ offers at roughly $50-150K a month. Inflo advises testing one funnel with about $1K of spend over 30 days. A June 2026 Inflo post recommends a hybrid, with a VSL for cold traffic and a weekly webinar for warm traffic, but its own figures conflict between posts. For live webinars generally, Livestorm (2025 data, 7M registrations, mostly B2B) reports a 47.7% live show-up rate. Half of registrations arrive in the final 7 days and 15% on the day itself. Viewers watch about 26 of 68 minutes on average, and Tuesday has the best show-up rate.
findings.why_it_matters: The '90-day plan' builder needs a funnel recommender driven by offer price, audience warmth, team capacity and lead volume, with set test budgets and decision dates. Webinar reminder and registration timing explain why last-week ad spend and day-of reminders matter.

findings.title: Low-ticket and challenge front ends for creator communities: $7-47 paid challenge, then a community upsell, on a page the operator controls
findings.detail: AdvLaunch, an agency that grows paid communities (updated Jul 2026), describes a four-step model. Meta ads send traffic to a 5-7 day paid challenge ($7-47), a 60-90 minute webinar or a 30-45 minute masterclass. The front end must deliver a concrete result. Completers are then offered the community at a founder rate. Retention is tracked by entry route. It insists on a landing page the operator controls rather than the Skool or Whop signup page, so pixel and server-side events fire correctly. It admits that conversion, CAC and churn benchmarks are its own assumptions. In its case study, one of eight ads produced about 84% of 3,403 applications. Vendor 'benchmarks' for paid challenges (CommuniPass) claim 75-85% completion and 30-45% upsell. These figures are unverified.
findings.why_it_matters: The low-ticket-to-high-ticket path needs entry-route attribution, server-side event setup and churn tracking by cohort. Heavy concentration of results in one creative supports a creative-testing workflow that finds and scales winners.

findings.title: How agencies sell the first 90 days: a productised build live in 14-30 days, followed by optimisation
findings.detail: These are vendor claims. Konvert says its steps 1-9 go live within 14 days: market and competitor research; ad scripts, production and campaign setup; landing page; VSL script, edit and hosting; qualifying form (Typeform, conditional logic, CRM sync); confirmation page with FAQ videos; pixel and custom events plus retargeting audiences; email sequences; and a pre-call SMS flow. Scaling then runs from about day 16 to day 90. The creator records about 2 hours a month, and founder-led video is the default with UGC (user-generated content) as an extra. Scaling With Systems starts with a diagnostic call to find the client's biggest bottleneck. It then builds the offer, VSL funnel with qualification, a pre-call 'trust' thank-you page, 30 days of automated pre-call email and SMS, ads, a sales script and a KPI dashboard, all live within 30 days. Its in-house ad tool applies rules such as scaling a budget by 50% when cost per call is well under target and killing an ad set at 0.4x ROAS. It guarantees at least 15 qualified calls in 90 days, subject to ad-spend minimums. The client spends about 1-2 hours a week plus their own sales calls. Both firms' disclaimers say results are not typical.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the deliverable list an Operator AI '90-day launch' template should produce and track, with approval gates on creative, copy and spend. Rules-based ad decisions such as scale or kill on cost per call and ROAS are an obvious fit for agents that propose and a person approves.

findings.title: Early churn: a cited 43% of B2B client churn happens in the first 90 days, and fast, written onboarding is the main lever
findings.detail: GigRadar (Apr 2026) cites Moxo's 2026 State of Churn report for this figure: 43% of B2B client churn happens within 90 days. Clients who finish intake within 48 hours reportedly keep above 85% retention at 12 months, against below 50% when intake takes over 10 days. When a client's champion leaves, the risk of churn within 12 months is 51%, rising to 65% for an executive. Recommended practice: send a welcome within 2 hours of signing; put scope, KPIs, baseline numbers, communication cadence, approval paths and a 30/60/90 roadmap in writing; check in on day 3; deliver a visible win between days 30 and 90; and review lost accounts for expectations set during the sale.
findings.why_it_matters: This sets up an onboarding agent for each new creator client: intake form, baseline snapshot (needed for rev share), written KPI and scope agreement, and a day-3 and day-30 health check. A 'first win' tracker targets the period when churn is highest.

sources.publisher: GigRadar (vendor blog, citing Moxo and Swydo)

findings.title: Why clients churn: budget, internal changes and lack of perceived value lead; poor onboarding expectations and attribution also feature
findings.detail: The AgencyAnalytics 2026 benchmarks survey (n=494, run Feb-Apr 2026) gives these churn drivers: budget cuts or economic pressure 42%, client-side internal changes 37%, lack of perceived value over time 32%, performance below expectations 31%, expectations misaligned at onboarding 24%, fee sensitivity 15%, unclear attribution or ROI 10%, and communication or trust 9%. 62% of clients stay 2+ years. Swydo data, cited elsewhere, ranks 'no proactive strategic guidance' (68%) and poor communication (57%) above price (37%). For growth operators specifically, reviewers warn that income rests on a few clients and that rev-share pay drops when the creator's marketing underperforms.
findings.why_it_matters: Churn-prevention features should make value visible: proactive weekly recommendations, attributed revenue, and early warnings when a client's internal situation changes or their KPIs fall. This matters more for operators who depend on 1-3 creator clients.

findings.title: Reporting is monthly for most agencies, and AI report drafting is the top time-saver, alongside more human review
findings.detail: AgencyAnalytics 2026 reports these figures. Report cadence: 69% monthly, 11% weekly, 8% bi-weekly, and only 5% offer a live dashboard. 73% produce a client report in under an hour, but 27% take 1 to 4+ hours. About 79-80% save 5+ hours a week with AI, and 35% save 10+ hours. Reports and performance summaries are the top AI benefit (42%). 38% use agentic AI for internal workflows. 58% have increased human review of AI-generated work.
findings.why_it_matters: The market backs both auto-drafted reports and the approval-gated design (human review is rising). High-ticket sales teams also need a weekly or daily cadence, which the monthly agency norm does not cover.

findings.title: Salespeople lose about 60% of their time to non-selling admin, which is the main case for setter and closer automation
findings.detail: Salesforce's 2026 sales statistics say reps spend about 60% of their time on non-selling work such as CRM notes, finding materials and chasing approvals. Some secondary sources cite 70%, which I could not verify. A 2026 Gartner survey, as reported, found AI saves sellers about 4.8 hours a week, but 72% of sales organisations put little of that time back into selling.
findings.why_it_matters: Auto-logging DM and call outcomes, drafting follow-ups and producing EOD (end-of-day) reports for setters and closers are high-value targets. The Gartner point suggests the product should also send the time saved into more conversations, for example by creating follow-up queues.

findings.title: Setter and closer roles, activity levels and pay: activity-based setter base, per-show bonus, close commission with refund clawbacks
findings.detail: Pay models: Coachingsales.com (Jul 2026) describes a setter base of $2-4K a month tied to activity KPIs (DMs sent, dials, dialer hours), $50-150 per qualified show, 2-5% of deal value per close, a 60/40 or 70/30 base-to-variable split, and clawback when a deal is refunded within 30 days or the lead was clearly unqualified. Activity levels: a setter-closer playbook (SetSmart, undated) describes setters spending 4-6 hours a day on 30-50 Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger conversations. Qualifying takes 5-15 messages covering situation, goals, timeline, past attempts and budget, and setters hand notes to the closer. Closers take 3-8 calls a day on a structured 30-60 minute call and are paid 10-20% commission when experienced. Other 2026 guides put closer commission at 8-15% of gross or cash collected, often with no base. Several vendors argue AI setters now replace part of the setter role.
findings.why_it_matters: The setter and closer modules need several pieces: an activity log, set-to-show and show-to-close tracking for each rep, structured handoff notes, a commission and clawback calculator based on cash collected and refunds, and coaching and training content for new reps.

findings.title: Show-rate and speed-to-lead tactics are the cheapest lever and are easy to automate
findings.detail: Recommended practices: confirm across more than one channel, allow one-tap rescheduling, shorten the gap between booking and the call, and mention the prospect's stated problem in reminders (Leads Now AI, Aug 2026). Send reminders at 48h, 24h and 2h, with no more than 3-4 touches (Inflo, Sep 2026). Leads Now AI's worked example is that lifting show rate from 60% to 80% adds about a third more real conversations at no extra ad spend. The speed-to-lead evidence is still the 2011 HBR study (contact within an hour made qualification roughly 7x more likely), which is old and covers all industries. Vendors pitch AI setters for instant reply and multi-touch follow-up, but say they should qualify and book, not sell.
findings.why_it_matters: A no-show prevention agent (personalised reminders, rescheduling, re-booking no-shows) and an instant-response qualification agent with human escalation are high-ROI, low-risk automations. Approval gates belong on the message templates, not on every send.

findings.title: GoHighLevel is the default all-in-one hub, and in 2026 it added metered AI employees, scheduled 'Super Agents', a unified client portal and a Claude MCP endpoint
findings.detail: Base plans are $97, $297 and $497 a month, plus usage fees (GHL Scale Up, pricing checked Aug 2026). HighLevel's official AI pricing: pay-per-use; AI Employee Growth at $50 a month per location (1,000 Conversation AI responses, 100 Voice AI minutes); Unlimited at $97 a month. Voice engine costs $0.045 a minute plus TTS, LLM and phone charges. Premium workflow AI actions cost $0.01 each. Funnel AI, Workflow AI builder, Email AI and Knowledge Base are free under fair use. July 2026 releases, as reported: Super Agents that run on a schedule or on CRM triggers, with MCP connectors (Make, Fathom, Calendly, Canva, OpenArt) and AI audit logs; a unified client portal combining courses, communities, dashboards, billing and files; resellable AI Employee tiers for agencies; multi-bot channel management; and an OAuth MCP endpoint for Claude.ai and Claude Code. Reviews call GHL a strong sales and follow-up engine but only average for course delivery.
findings.why_it_matters: GHL is both the incumbent Operator AI must integrate with and its most direct competitor for an 'agentic' all-in-one white-label product. Operator AI's edge has to come from coaching-specific workflows (setter and closer, rev-share, student training) and approval gating, not from basic CRM, funnels or AI chat.

findings.title: iClosed: a scheduler for high-ticket funnels that qualifies and routes leads before they book
findings.detail: Vendor claims (page dated 14 Oct 2026). iClosed captures leads before they book and screens them, including credit-score and debt-to-income checks against offer price rules. It routes buyers to top closers by offer, geography or intent, and sends unqualified leads to a URL without firing the ad pixel. It offers a unified inbox (iMessage, WhatsApp, SMS, email) with owner assignment, texts drop-offs within seconds, runs SMS and email no-show workflows, tracks call outcomes and pushes them to the CRM, and calculates close rate from incoming payments. It integrates with Hyros and GHL and has a REST API and webhooks. It claims use by 20,000 high-ticket funnels and says only 3 in 10 leads book from a typical scheduler. Target users are coaches, info-product sellers and agencies running VSL, webinar and challenge funnels.
findings.why_it_matters: Qualification and routing before booking, and keeping disqualified leads out of the ad pixel, are now standard expectations. Operator AI should match them or integrate. Credit screening raises fair-lending and privacy questions that suit an approval gate.

findings.title: Attribution, call review and dialer tools in the stack: Hyros for ad and sales attribution, Close for calling and call coaching
findings.detail: Hyros (vendor claims, page dated 26 Oct 2026) targets courses, coaching and webinars. It attributes booked calls and closed deals, sends sales the ad platforms missed back to Meta and Google to improve targeting, and demos a Claude MCP connection that ranks ad sets by ROAS and LTV and proposes changes. Its headline and sample figures on 'missed' sales do not match. Close (vendor claims, undated coaching page) offers call recording and transcription, live listen, whisper and barge, tagging of standout calls, activity and conversion reporting, and shared SMS and email templates for ramping new reps. Live coaching sits on the Enterprise plan. Third-party reviews describe its power and predictive dialers.
findings.why_it_matters: Two jobs are table stakes: attributing cash collected (not leads) back to ad and creative, and reviewing recorded calls for coaching. Hyros already demos AI agents that change ad budgets, so Operator AI's approval-gated version needs clear audit trails to stand out.

findings.title: Community and course platform fees change rev-share economics: Skool, Whop, Kajabi and ClickFunnels
findings.detail: Third-party 2026 guides report the following. Skool: Hobby at $9 a month with 10% + 30c per transaction; Pro at $99 a month with 2.9% + 30c, with some reporting about 3.9% on sales above roughly $900. A Skool-referral ('Growth Boost') commission of 30% is reported but disputed. Whop: about 2.7-3% + 30c, with a built-in affiliate programme defaulting to 30%. Kajabi: $179, $249 or $499 a month. ClickFunnels: $97, $197 or $297 a month. Circle's 2026 survey (vendor; sample not stated) found 88% of community creators monetise through memberships, 53% through courses and 51% through coaching or services. It also found 48% run their communities solo and 27% use six or more tools.
findings.why_it_matters: Rev-share statements must net out platform, processor and affiliate fees, and they should state whether the split is on gross or net. Creators running solo on many tools are exactly the buyers who need an operator, and the operator then needs one consolidated view.

findings.title: Meta ads in 2026: Andromeda retrieval rewards high-volume, varied creative in consolidated campaigns, so creative production is a weekly job
findings.detail: Meta Engineering (Dec 2024) describes Andromeda as the ML system that picks a few thousand candidate ads from tens of millions. Meta reports +6% recall and +8% ad quality on selected segments. Agencies in 2026 say this favours broad targeting, fewer ad sets and many genuinely different creatives rather than duplicates. Segwise cites internal Meta testing in which one ad set with 25 creatives beat five ad sets of five, with 17% more conversions at 16% lower cost, and claims advertisers testing 20+ new ads a month get higher ROAS. These figures are unverified. WSJ-based reports said Meta aimed to fully automate ad creation and targeting by the end of 2026, but I found no official rollout schedule.
findings.why_it_matters: Creative ideation, scripting, founder-recorded and UGC production, tagging and win/loss analysis is a large and recurring time sink. An approval-gated creative pipeline (briefs, hooks, variants, naming and tagging, performance read-back) is a strong agent use case.

findings.title: ManyChat (comment-to-DM) reportedly changed pricing in 2026, but sources conflict
findings.detail: Several 2026 third-party guides say ManyChat changed pricing on 2 Mar 2026. They report the free plan cut to about 25 active contacts, new Essential and Pro tiers (for example, from $14 for 250 contacts and from $29 for 2,500), per-contact overage fees, and AI as a paid add-on (one source says $29 a month). Other sources still list older pricing or say AI is included in Pro. Everyone agrees comment-triggered DM automation remains the core Instagram feature, and reviewers describe ManyChat's AI as mostly guided and rule-based. I found no official announcement.
findings.why_it_matters: Comment-to-DM lead capture is a standard top-of-funnel step for creator clients. Rising cost and limited AI give Operator AI room to bundle compliant comment-to-DM flows into AI setter handoff, within Meta's window and disclosure rules.

findings.title: The growth-operator model is criticised for unverified income claims and creator-side economics, which bears on the programme's own positioning
findings.detail: Critical reviews say leading growth-operator programmes lack transparency, publish income claims ($20-50K a month from 1-3 clients) that cannot be verified, and oversell AI. Beginners cannot run a back end with AI alone, and finding and closing creators remains a human sales job. They cite MBO Partners data that 71% of creators earn under $30K a year, which means many creators cannot afford an operator. Reddit and YouTube reviews are mixed, with many reporting no income yet. Independent context from the 2025 ICF and PwC Global Coaching Study: about 123K coach practitioners worldwide, and 60% expect growth from more clients rather than higher fees (37%).
findings.why_it_matters: Operator AI is white-labelled for a programme in this category. Built-in honest metrics (student pipeline, signed clients, verified revenue) and claim-substantiation tooling reduce regulatory and reputational risk and can become a selling point for the programme owner.

findings.title: Weekly operating rhythm (synthesis): daily sales activity, weekly KPI and creative review, monthly client report and rev-share settlement, 90-day re-plan
findings.detail: This rhythm is put together from the sources above. Daily: setters work 30-50 DM conversations and log EODs; closers take 3-8 calls with notes and outcomes; new leads get a reply within minutes; reminders go out at 48h, 24h and 2h; ad spend is checked against cost-per-call and ROAS rules. Weekly: team KPI review (booking, show and close by source and rep), call-recording review and coaching, creative review with new variants briefed and launched, a creator content and recording session (about 2 hours a month to 1-2 hours a week, by vendor), and pipeline hygiene. Monthly: client report (69% of agencies report monthly), cash collected against baseline, rev-share and commission reconciliation after refunds and clawbacks, and a strategy recommendation, since lack of proactive guidance is a leading churn reason. Quarterly or every 90 days: offer and funnel re-audit, next test plan and a renewal conversation.
findings.why_it_matters: This maps directly to scheduled, approval-gated agents and role views: setter (daily queue), closer (call prep and notes), coach (weekly review), owner (monthly P&L and rev share) and student (learning the rhythm with live data).

findings.title: Jobs-to-be-done checklist for a growth operator, and the time sinks software can remove (synthesis)
findings.detail:
Checklist, put together from all sources above.

A. Pick a niche and land clients: (1) choose a niche and write the ICP; (2) build a list of creators and experts and score them for fit and account health; (3) research each and draft a personalised opener; (4) work multi-touch outreach and follow-up within platform limits; (5) run discovery and partnership calls; (6) propose terms (retainer, rev share, baseline, ad-spend owner, term) and sign.

B. Onboard (days 0-14): (7) intake within 48h, access to accounts (ads, pixel, CRM, payments, community), baseline revenue snapshot; (8) audit offer, funnel and sales (pages, follow-up, show and close); (9) written KPIs and a 30/60/90 roadmap.

C. Build (days 1-30): (10) build or fix the offer ladder (low ticket, challenge or community, high ticket); (11) choose the funnel (VSL, webinar, challenge, application, DM-to-call); (12) copy, VSL and webinar scripts, landing and confirmation pages; (13) qualifying form, routing and calendar; (14) pixel and server-side events, UTMs and attribution; (15) email and SMS nurture plus pre-call sequences, with consent and opt-out logging; (16) comment-to-DM and DM-setting flows with bot disclosure; (17) checkout, payment plans, financing, refund policy; (18) claims and testimonial substantiation review.

D. Team (days 15-60): (19) hire, script and train setters and closers; (20) EOD reports, call recording and review; (21) commission and clawback plan.

E. Run and scale (days 30-90+): (22) creative briefs, production and testing; (23) daily spend rules; (24) weekly KPI review; (25) no-show recovery and database reactivation; (26) monthly client report, rev-share settlement, and churn-risk and renewal signals.

Biggest time sinks seen in sources: prospect research and personalised outreach; DM triage and follow-up; no-show chasing; manual CRM logging (about 60% of rep time is non-selling); building reports (27% of agencies take 1h+ per report); creative volume under Andromeda; call review; commission and rev-share reconciliation; access and tool setup across 6+ tools.
findings.why_it_matters: This gives a direct backlog for Operator AI's agents and approval gates, ordered by when the work happens. The steps with legal exposure (claims, consent, bot disclosure, credit screening, rev-share settlement) should always require human approval.

open_questions: Research stopped early: the shared web-search budget for this run ran out (200 calls). Meta's advertising standards on income claims and get-rich-quick offers, and UK and EU rules on earnings claims (CMA, ASA), were not checked.

No credible public data exists on growth-operator client acquisition: how many outreach touches it takes to sign one creator, or the close rate on partnership calls. Programme-owner or anonymised in-product data would be needed.
Real rev-share contract terms are undocumented publicly: gross vs net, refund and chargeback handling, who pays ad spend, minimum term, buyout and IP or community ownership if the creator leaves.
The status in 2026 of the FTC's January 2025 proposal to extend the Business Opportunity Rule to business coaching and online courses was not confirmed against the Federal Register.
Conflicting reports were not resolved: Skool Pro's fee above roughly $900 (2.9% vs 3.9%), ManyChat's March 2026 pricing and AI add-on, and a reported 27 Apr 2026 Meta message-tag change.
The webinar show-up benchmarks (Livestorm, Univid) come mostly from B2B events. Coaching and creator webinar or challenge attendance data is vendor-only and unverified.
No churn data is specific to creator-operator partnerships (as opposed to marketing agencies in general), and no data shows how often creators take the back end in-house after 6-12 months.

checks.title: Growth operator scope: core objects (creator client, offer ladder, funnel, community/product, ad account, sales team, tracking)
checks.evidence: clients table plus COLUMN_MIGRATIONS (operator_ai/db.py: niche, offer, price, retainer, kpi_targets, access.ad_account_id, brief). client_ops.py: start_onboarding (access checklist, intake link, kickoff draft), weekly_ops (numbers, diagnostic, ad proposals, weekly report, monthly review), churn_signals. agents/fulfilment.py fulfil. Missions client_onboarding and client_weekly_ops (missions/templates.py). The run-the-back-end loop exists.
checks.gap: No offer-ladder object: each client has one offer and one price. No funnel, community or product object (Skool, Whop or course). The creator's own sales team is not modelled: setter and closer in auth.ROLES are the programme's staff. Tracking is weekly aggregate client_metrics only. Confirmed bug: proposals.accept calls prospects.mark_won(price=chosen option amount, offer=option label). That writes the operator's retainer or pilot fee into clients.price, which the UI labels 'Their offer price ($)' (web/src/pages/Clients.tsx:417), and writes 'Monthly retainer' into clients.offer. fulfilment.fulfil (line 93: price = cl['price'] or ...) and client_ops.weekly_ops (line 845: offer_price = cl['price']) then treat the operator's fee as the creator's offer price. As a result, the VSL outline price line, the money model and the bottleneck money impact are wrong for every client won through a proposal. Also, start_onboarding never copies the prospect's real offer, because clients.offer is already set.

checks.title: Deal structures: retainer, rev share, hybrid, setup fees; baseline, attribution and settlement ledger
checks.evidence: proposals.py options_for offers three options: retainer; 'Lower retainer + performance share' (performance_pct default 10, max 50, on net cash collected above a baseline agreed in week one); paid pilot. build_sections terms define net cash as cash received less refunds, chargebacks, processing fees and sales tax, paid monthly on instalments collected, with refunds netted on the next statement. Ad spend is paid by the client. Public e-accept page at /t/<tid>/p/<token>.
checks.gap: Accepted terms are not stored on the client: clients has only 'retainer', with no performance_pct, baseline value or period, attribution source or term. There is no baseline-capture step, no monthly settlement statement or reconciliation ledger, and no cash-collected source of truth (client_metrics.revenue is hand-entered or from CSV). There is no dispute workflow for contested 'incremental' revenue. Platform and affiliate fees are not in the net definition. The same mark_won price/offer conflation applies (see the scope item).

checks.title: Niche and prospect qualification: ICP scorecard, account health, approved openers, follow-up cap, pipeline
checks.evidence: prospects.py has a per-user ICP (get_icp/save_icp: niche, price band, audience band, must-haves, disqualifiers, signals) and a transparent fit score with per-factor reasons (score). Imports require a lawful basis. Research facts carry sources. opener_variants plus the unverified_personalisation guard block facts that are not in the research. Every draft goes to the approval queue. FOLLOWUP_DAYS=[2,4,7]. STAGES run new to won, lost, nurture or dnc. move_stats reports Wilson CIs per opener move.
checks.gap: No account-health check (overnight follower spikes, engagement drops, fake followers); fit uses only a follower-count band. No 'engage first' (comment before DM) step. Follow-up count is fixed at 3. No cross-tenant anonymised conversion benchmarks: move_stats is per tenant, and pooling would need consent and an aggregation design.

checks.title: Cold Instagram DM pacing, warm-up and action-block risk
checks.evidence: queue.MANUAL_CHANNELS includes instagram_dm, so cold DMs are always awaiting_manual_send: a person sends them from their own app and confirms 'I sent it'. prospects.DEFAULT_CAPS dm=20/day per user counts confirmed sends plus waiting first messages, and the daily_cap guardrail rechecks at approval. Playbook first-client-outreach instagram-dm-outreach-norms-and-limits.
checks.gap: Caps are per user, not per Instagram account. No warm-up by account age. There is no way to record an action block and no auto-pause after one. No near-duplicate check across a day's openers.

checks.title: Meta Messenger/IG messaging policy: 24h window, manual-only Human Agent tag, no promos in tags, bot disclosure, 30s responses
checks.evidence: Nothing sends through the IG or Messenger API. Every IG and FB DM is human-sent (queue.MANUAL_CHANNELS; SELF_SCORE says Meta app review is needed). Inbound IG replies are pasted in (inbound.CAPTURE_CHANNELS). The rules are documented in playbook content-organic-email instagram-comment-to-dm-messaging-rules.
checks.gap: Not applicable while all DMs stay human-sent. If an automated DM setter or comment-to-DM is ever built, none of the following exists in code: window timers, a manual-only Human Agent path, a no-promotions-in-tags check, first-message bot disclosure, or response-time monitoring.

checks.title: EU AI Act Art. 50 chatbot disclosure (applied 2 Aug 2026)
checks.evidence: persona/apply.py answers 'I'm an AI assistant trained on X's material, not X' when asked. Styled public answers carry a badge and disclosure (console.py:355). The phone line uses only neutral TTS voices (channels.NEUTRAL_TTS_VOICES); no cloning. Outbound prospect text is human-approved before sending.
checks.gap: Not compliant at two public touchpoints. The phone Q&A greeting is 'Hi, ask me anything about the programme.' (channels.py:590), with no AI disclosure. The public lead-magnet mini page (routes/channels.py:140 MINI_HTML) says 'Answers come only from the programme's material' but never says the visitor is talking to an AI. Both contradict the playbook's own step that every AI chat or voice agent must say it is an AI in its first message. There is no synthetic-media label field on ad or creative drafts; that is acceptable while nothing generates a likeness.

checks.title: TCPA revoke-all (now 31 Jan 2027): cross-channel opt-out registry
checks.evidence: inbound.py OPT_OUT_WORDS (STOP, STOPALL, UNSUBSCRIBE, CANCEL, END, QUIT, OPTOUT, REVOKE) plus natural-language phrasings. apply_dnc sets party-level do_not_contact, suppresses every known address (email, handle, phone) through delivery.suppress, opts out SMS and phone together, and holds all open items. Guardrails do_not_contact, unsubscribed and not_opted_in block on every channel. Playbook compliance-2026 tcpa-consent-revocation-2025 already records 31 Jan 2027.
checks.gap: Consent and opt-out state is spread across contact_points.opted_in, channel_links, suppressions and audit. There is no single exportable consent-ledger view for proof.

checks.title: FTC earnings, growth and refund-guarantee claims (Air AI, Ascend, BizOpp NPRM)
checks.evidence: guardrails.py blocks income_claim, guarantee, fake_testimonial and unverified_result in every mode. claims.py proof records (evidence files, typicality note of at least 20 characters, expiry) gate the only allowed figure. Intake captures proof_permission. Playbook compliance-2026 covers Air AI, Growth Cave and the BizOpp NPRM.
checks.gap: call_review.review scores stages, objections and discounting only. It runs no guardrail pass on call transcripts, so income or guarantee promises on calls go unflagged. No record of refund or guarantee terms, or of whether refunds were honoured: refund requests only escalate to the owner (escalations.OWNER_RESOLVES). Get-rich-quick phrasing passes (see the processor item).

checks.title: Payment processor prohibitions (Stripe 'fast, easy money'), refund and chargeback monitoring
checks.evidence: I ran guardrails.check on three sentences: 'Make fast, easy money from your laptop with no experience needed', 'Quit your 9-5 and build passive income in 30 days' and 'Get rich quick with our system'. All three returned no flags in both outreach and client_asset mode, and rubrics.score('ad') gave the first one 99/100. console.payment_webhook is a signed mock that only grants member access: it records no amounts and no disputes. Dispute thresholds exist only in playbook text (fulfilment-retention-ops card-network-dispute-thresholds).
checks.gap: Missing pieces: a get-rich-quick / 'no experience' / 'passive income' rule; refund-rate and chargeback-rate (VAMP) monitoring; a pre-launch policy review. Conversely, an objective refund policy ('30-day refund policy: if you attend every session ... full refund') is blocked as 'guarantee', so compliant refund terms cannot be drafted at all.

checks.title: High-ticket funnel KPIs: booking, show and close by source and rep; cost per booked call by price tier; triage
checks.evidence: diagnostic.STAGES use SOP benchmarks: reply 10%, conversation 40%, link 50%, booked 30%, show 60%, close 20%, webinar stages, CPL $15. The diagnostic computes money impact and names one bottleneck with a fix. client_ops.kpi_status feeds the weekly report.
checks.gap: No application-to-booking stage. No breakdown by source or rep: leads.source exists but the diagnostic takes totals, and leads have no rep. No cost per booked or showed call against the price tier. No 4-6 week trend judgement and no allowance for a new rep's ramp. The CPL ceiling is stale (see out_of_date).

checks.title: Funnel recommender for the 90-day plan (VSL, webinar, application, hybrid) by price, warmth, capacity and volume
checks.evidence: fulfilment.fulfil _plan is the same fixed 4-week list for every client: Thunder Dome, then 24h/2h/10min reminders, then a seven-segment webinar outline, then launch. studio.launch_kit drafts every line regardless of fit.
checks.gap: No recommender driven by offer price, audience warmth, team capacity or lead volume. No test budget or decision dates.

checks.title: Low-ticket, challenge and community front ends with entry-route attribution and server-side events
checks.evidence: No product, challenge or community (Skool/Whop) object. webinars.register stores a registrant 'source'. client_ops CHECKLIST has a hand-ticked 'Pixel and Conversions API' item. Playbook webinars-vsl-funnels challenge-funnels exists as text only.
checks.gap: Missing: attribution from entry route to purchase, CAPI/server-side event setup or verification, churn by entry-route cohort, and a low-ticket checkout step.

checks.title: Productised 90-day launch (live in 14-30 days) with rules-based spend decisions
checks.evidence: proposals build_sections has a 30/60/90 plan and deliverables. client_ops CHECKLIST: intake, Meta partner access, pixel/CAPI, CRM, calendar, domain, kickoff. fulfilment: money model, reviewed hooks, VSL outline, launch plan. webinar_chain: offer, titles, slide script, registration and thank-you pages, show-up and replay sequences. ads_ops.propose_changes queues kill-on-CPL pause proposals that the owner approves; creates stay PAUSED and can be rolled back.
checks.gap: No qualifying-form builder with conditional logic. No confirmation page with FAQ. No pre-call SMS flow for the client's own funnel. No deliverable tracker with dates against a 14- or 30-day go-live. No scale rule, and no cost-per-call or ROAS rule, because nothing attributes CRM outcomes back to ads.

Playbook content-organic-email instagram-messaging-rate-limits says the CONFIRMED_EVENT_UPDATE, ACCOUNT_UPDATE and POST_PURCHASE_UPDATE tags errored from 27 Apr 2026. That falls short of the Stripe restricted-businesses list (updated 22 Sep 2026), Meta's get-rich-quick policy and the FTC action against Air AI (Mar 2026).

findings.title: Meta Messenger/Instagram: AI may only send freely inside the 24-hour window; the Human Agent tag is for a person typing, and three utility tags stopped working on 2026-04-27
findings.detail: Meta's Send API docs (v26.0 era, undated) say the standard messaging window is usually 24 hours from the user's last action. It can stretch to 7 days after a first message that follows a Click-to-Messenger or Click-to-Direct ad. Promotional content is allowed inside the window. Outside it, a business may only send tagged, non-promotional messages. The Human Agent tag lets a business representative reply manually within 7 days, and Meta describes it as manual, human-operated replies; several vendor guides say using it for bot messages breaks policy. Starting 27 April 2026, API calls that use CONFIRMED_EVENT_UPDATE, ACCOUNT_UPDATE or POST_PURCHASE_UPDATE return error code 100. Meta's suggested promotional alternatives are Sponsored Messages and One-Time Notifications. Meta warns that misusing tags can restrict a Page's or account's ability to message.
findings.why_it_matters: Each thread needs a window clock tied to the last inbound message (24h, or 7 days for ad-originated threads). After expiry, AI-drafted sends should be blocked automatically. The Human Agent tag should be allowed only when a named setter or closer writes or edits the message and sends it, and the audit log should record that human. Webinar reminders and booking confirmations should not use the removed tags; route them through opt-in notifications or SMS/email.

findings.title: Instagram comment-to-DM (private replies): one message per commenter, sent within 7 days; follow-ups only after a reply
findings.detail: Meta's Instagram Platform docs say a private reply can be sent to someone who commented on a post, reel, story, ad or Live. Only one message can go to the commenter, and it must be sent within 7 days of the comment. On Live, it can only be sent during the broadcast. Further messages are allowed only after the person responds, and within 24 hours of that response. The reply lands in the Inbox if the person follows the account, otherwise in Requests. It requires a professional account, comments webhooks, and the instagram_business_manage_comments or instagram_manage_messages permissions. Vendor guides add two claims I could not check against Meta: that the official API offers no compliant way to cold-DM people who never interacted, and that Meta's spam policies forbid requiring a like, share or follow before giving promised content. One vendor also cites a rate limit of about 750 private replies per hour.
findings.why_it_matters: The comment-trigger builder should allow one opener per commenter, with no drip sequence until the lead replies. It should drop triggers older than 7 days, reject 'follow to get the link' gating, and pace sends below rate limits. Outbound DM prospecting by students to people who never engaged should be handled as manual, human-sent work outside the API, not automated.

findings.title: Meta automated-chat requirements: a human escalation path and a bot disclosure where the law requires it
findings.detail: Meta's Instagram Messaging overview requires every app to offer an escalation path to a human agent. Automation can run as a single app with a custom inbox, or as several apps using the Handover Protocol. Where the law requires it, the automated chat must say it is automated at the start of the conversation, after a significant lapse, and when a chat moves from a human to automation. Meta names California and German users specifically and recommends disclosure everywhere as best practice, for example 'You are talking to a bot'. Instagram Requests-folder conversations inactive for 30 days are no longer returned by the API.
findings.why_it_matters: Every AI DM agent needs three things built in: an always-available 'talk to a human' handoff that routes to the setter or closer queue, an automatic disclosure line at the start and on bot takeover, and a stale-conversation rule for Requests threads.

findings.title: WhatsApp Business terms bar general-purpose AI assistants from 15 Jan 2026; business-specific sales and support bots are still allowed
findings.detail: Meta added an 'AI providers' section to the WhatsApp Business Solution terms, announced in October 2025. It applied to new users from 15 October 2025 and to existing users from 15 January 2026. It stops AI model providers from using the Business API to distribute assistants whose core function is general-purpose AI, and Meta decides what counts as the primary use. Meta told TechCrunch the change targets AI assistant distributors, not businesses using AI for customer service. Vendor analysis says structured bots for support, bookings, notifications and sales remain allowed. EU, Italian and Brazilian regulators have reportedly opened antitrust probes.
findings.why_it_matters: Each WhatsApp agent in Operator AI should be scoped to the client business's own offer: qualification, booking, FAQs and onboarding. It should not be presented as an open-ended 'ask me anything' assistant. A topic guardrail and a scope description should be stored for each tenant in case Meta reviews it.

findings.title: LinkedIn User Agreement (effective 3 Nov 2025) bans bots for connecting, messaging, engagement and scraping; LinkedIn enforces it in court
findings.detail: Section 8.2 of LinkedIn's User Agreement (effective 3 Nov 2025) prohibits several things. These include bots or other unauthorised automated methods to add or download contacts, send or redirect messages, or comment, like or share. It also bans software that scrapes or copies profiles, bypassing use limits, and deceptive manipulated media. LinkedIn's Help Center says third-party crawlers, bots and browser extensions that scrape or automate activity breach the agreement, and restricted members must uninstall them before being reinstated. LinkedIn sued the scraping API Proxycurl in January 2025, citing fake accounts and scraping. Proxycurl shut down by July 2025, and a permanent injunction was reportedly entered. Vendor claims of a 2026 detection surge (for example '23% restriction within 90 days') are unsourced.
findings.why_it_matters: Operator AI should not automate sending on LinkedIn (connects, DMs, likes, comments) and should not ship or recommend scraping extensions or LinkedIn-scraped enrichment data. For LinkedIn, the safe pattern is AI drafts plus human copy-and-send, with a human-sent flag and per-user volume coaching. Every enrichment source should be checked for LinkedIn-derived data.

findings.title: Gmail sender rules: stricter enforcement since Nov 2025, with temporary and permanent rejections for non-compliant mail
findings.detail: All senders to Gmail need SPF or DKIM, valid forward and reverse DNS, TLS, RFC 5322 formatting, and a Postmaster spam rate below 0.3%. Bulk senders (over 5,000 messages a day to personal Gmail) also need SPF, DKIM and DMARC. DMARC p=none is acceptable, but the From: domain must align with the SPF or DKIM domain. Marketing and subscribed mail needs one-click unsubscribe (List-Unsubscribe-Post per RFC 8058) plus a visible unsubscribe link in the body, with unsubscribes honoured within 48 hours. Google's FAQ says that starting November 2025 Gmail is 'ramping up' enforcement on non-compliant traffic with temporary and permanent rejections, and new domains get faster enforcement. A sender whose spam rate goes above 0.3% loses mitigation eligibility until it has stayed below 0.3% for 7 consecutive days. Google recommends staying under 0.1%.
findings.why_it_matters: Operator AI needs a sending preflight for each tenant and domain: SPF, DKIM, DMARC alignment, PTR and TLS checks. It should inject RFC 8058 headers and a body link automatically, and push unsubscribes to suppression within 48 hours. Spam rate should be monitored from Postmaster with a warning at 0.1% and an automatic pause before 0.3%. New student domains need warm-up limits.

sources.publisher: Google Workspace Admin Help (sender guidelines FAQ)

findings.title: Yahoo bulk-sender rules: DMARC alignment, RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe, unsubscribes honoured within 2 days, complaints under 0.3%
findings.detail: Yahoo's Sender Hub requires all senders to have SPF or DKIM, valid forward and reverse DNS, RFC 5321/5322 compliance, and a spam rate below 0.3%. Bulk senders need both SPF and DKIM, DMARC of at least p=none that passes with relaxed alignment, a working List-Unsubscribe header that supports one-click unsubscribe (POST per RFC 8058 strongly recommended), and a visible unsubscribe link in the body. Unsubscribes must be processed within 2 days. Yahoo publishes no volume threshold, and it calculates spam rate against mail delivered to the inbox, so a sender's own figure will look lower. Enforcement began in February 2024 and was phased in during that year.
findings.why_it_matters: The unsubscribe SLA should be set to the strictest provider: within 2 days and preferably immediate. Because Yahoo has no volume threshold, compliance should not depend on volume; every cold or marketing send should carry the full authentication and unsubscribe stack.

findings.title: Microsoft Outlook.com high-volume sender rules in force since 5 May 2025; failures bounce with 550 5.7.515
findings.detail: Microsoft's Outlook team requires domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day to Outlook.com, Hotmail.com and Live.com to pass SPF and DKIM and to publish DMARC of at least p=none aligned with SPF or DKIM. They are also expected to use a compliant P2 sender address, offer a working unsubscribe, and keep lists clean. Enforcement began on 5 May 2025. The original announcement said non-compliant mail would go to Junk first, with rejection on a later date. Non-compliant mail is rejected with '550; 5.7.515 Access denied, sending domain does not meet the required authentication level'. A secondary source updated in October 2026 says Microsoft's announcement now specifies rejection while its Postmaster policies still describe junking before rejection. Check bounce logs rather than assuming a junk-folder grace period.
findings.why_it_matters: 5.7.515 should be treated as a hard authentication failure. Sending on that domain should stop automatically, and the tenant owner should get a DNS-fix task. The same authentication preflight covers Google, Yahoo and Microsoft, so one compliance gate can serve all three.

findings.title: CAN-SPAM covers B2B cold email; penalty up to $53,088 per email (2025 level kept for 2026); senders are liable for mail sent on their behalf
findings.detail: The FTC's CAN-SPAM guide says the Act 'makes no exception for business-to-business email'. Requirements: accurate header and routing information, non-deceptive subject lines, a clear statement that the message is an ad, a valid physical postal address, and a clear opt-out that works for at least 30 days after sending. Opt-outs must be honoured within 10 business days. Companies remain responsible for email others send on their behalf. Each violating email can draw up to $53,088. An FTC Federal Register notice says civil penalty amounts stay at 2025 levels for 2026, following OMB Memorandum M-26-11 cancelling the 2026 inflation adjustments.
findings.why_it_matters: In a white-label setup where students send for creator or expert clients, both the seller and the sender can be liable. Every outbound email needs a footer with the client's postal address and an opt-out. Suppression must be shared across all of a client's sender identities and mailboxes. Deceptive subject lines (fake 'Re:' or 'Fwd:') should be blocked in the approval gate.

findings.title: TCPA consent revocation: 'any reasonable means' and the 10-business-day rule have applied since April 2025; the FCC's Sept 2026 order lets callers choose an exclusive opt-out method; revoke-all is waived until 31 Jan 2027
findings.detail: The FCC's 2024 TCPA Consent Order took effect on 11 April 2025 (47 CFR 64.1200(a)(10)). Consumers can revoke consent to robocalls and robotexts by any reasonable means, including replying STOP or another word from a standard list, and callers must honour it within a reasonable time of no more than 10 business days. The 'revoke all' piece makes an opt-out from one type of message apply to all of the caller's robocalls and texts. The Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau has waived it until 31 Jan 2027 (DA 26-12, 6 Jan 2026). An FCC draft Report and Order and FNPRM (FCC-CIRC 2609-05, fact sheet dated 9 Sept 2026; Day Pitney reports adoption on 30 Sept 2026) changes two things. Callers may designate one of three methods as the exclusive way to revoke: an automated IVR or key-press opt-out, a STOP-type reply text, or a website or phone number they provide. For informational robocalls only, a revocation may be treated as covering just that category. The FNPRM asks whether to cut the 10-business-day deadline to 7, require two-way texting, require a 'revoke all' method, and decide how revocation applies to affiliates. Marketing messages are not covered by the category carve-out.
findings.why_it_matters: The SMS layer needs a few rules. It should parse opt-out keywords and free-text opt-outs in every reply, apply them at once to all marketing from that tenant across SMS, AI voice and WhatsApp, and target same-day processing, well under the possible 7-day limit. Every message should state the designated opt-out method. Programme reminders (informational) should be kept separate from sales or marketing streams so that a scoped revocation can work if the new order takes effect.

findings.title: AI-generated voices count as 'artificial' under the TCPA: AI voice calls need prior express consent, and written consent for telemarketing
findings.detail: The FCC's February 2024 declaratory ruling treats calls using AI-generated or cloned voices as 'artificial or prerecorded voice' calls under the TCPA, effective immediately. This is not an outright ban. Such calls need prior express consent, or prior express written consent for telemarketing. They also carry the identification, disclosure and opt-out duties that apply to prerecorded calls. A secondary source claims further 2026 FCC action on AI-voice robocalls, which I could not confirm.
findings.why_it_matters: Any outbound AI voice agent for setters, such as speed-to-lead calls, no-show recovery or webinar reminders, should dial only numbers with stored written consent that names the seller. It should say at the start who is calling and on whose behalf, and offer an automated opt-out. Inbound and consented callbacks are the lower-risk setup.

findings.title: The FCC's one-to-one consent rule was vacated (11th Cir., 24 Jan 2025); bundled consent is allowed federally, but written consent must still be provable
findings.detail: The Eleventh Circuit (Insurance Marketing Coalition v. FCC) vacated the FCC's one-to-one consent rule one business day before its 27 January 2025 effective date. That rule would have required consent to name one seller at a time and that calls be topically related to the website where consent was given. The court held the FCC cannot add requirements the statute lacks. Commentators say the existing TCPA rules still apply and consent covering several sellers remains permissible. A 2026 vendor blog wrongly says the rule took effect on 27 Jan 2026, so lead-gen tooling vendors should be checked for this error.
findings.why_it_matters: Opt-in forms and lead magnets (webinar sign-ups, VSL opt-ins) should still capture prior express written consent for marketing texts and AI or prerecorded calls. Each record should keep the seller name, the disclosure text shown, a timestamp, IP and user agent, and the form version. The system should be able to prove consent for each client, because students run funnels for several creators.

findings.title: TCPA quiet hours (8am to 9pm recipient local time) drive text class actions; consent is the main defence (King v. Bon Charge, D. Del., 30 Apr 2026)
findings.detail: 47 CFR 64.1200(c)(1) bars telemarketing calls and, per courts and plaintiffs, texts to residential subscribers before 8am or after 9pm in the recipient's local time. Plaintiffs' firms have brought quiet-hours class actions even where consumers had opted in. In King v. Bon Charge (D. Del., 30 Apr 2026), the court held that a consumer who signed up for marketing texts could not bring a quiet-hours claim, because the consent need not be a signed written agreement. Courts are still split, an industry petition to the FCC (March 2025) is pending, and state laws can set stricter calling windows. Separately, courts disagree on whether texts are 'calls' after the Supreme Court's 2025 McLaughlin Chiropractic decision.
findings.why_it_matters: The SMS and voice scheduler should resolve each recipient's time zone from area code or stored address and send only inside a conservative window, for example 9am to 8pm local, to cover stricter state rules. Messages that fall outside it should queue rather than send. AI-triggered instant replies to inbound texts are the safer case because the consumer initiated them, but marketing broadcasts must respect the window.

findings.title: Texas SB 140 (effective 1 Sept 2025) puts marketing texts under Texas telemarketing law with a private right of action; consent-based programmes are outside registration
findings.detail: SB 140 extended Texas's 'telephone solicitation' definition (Bus. & Com. Code ch. 304 and related) to text, multimedia and image messages. It also gave consumers a direct private right of action under the DTPA, with possible treble and mental-anguish damages and attorney's fees. Sidley reports that covered sellers must register with the Texas Secretary of State, make disclosures, pay fees, and post a $10,000 security. After an industry lawsuit, the Texas Attorney General clarified (around November 2025) that consent-based text programmes are not subject to registration and disclosure, and the case was dismissed.
findings.why_it_matters: Texas numbers should require documented opt-in before any marketing text. Unconsented 'cold' SMS should be blocked for every state, and especially Texas, because of the private right of action. Consent provenance should be kept for each message to support the exemption.

findings.title: US A2P 10DLC: unregistered traffic has been blocked since Feb 2025; brand and campaign registration with opt-in evidence is a prerequisite
findings.detail: Provider documentation says major US carriers block 100% of unregistered 10DLC application-to-person traffic. Telnyx dates this from 3 February 2025, and a 2026 vendor guide says the policy still holds. Registration through The Campaign Registry needs a brand (EIN-matched), a campaign use case, sample messages, and a description of how opt-in is collected. 2026 vendor guides say carriers now reject or throttle misregistered traffic in real time rather than warning first. They also mention Authentication+ verification for public brands and higher fees, which I did not verify with TCR or the carriers.
findings.why_it_matters: Each tenant (creator client or student agency) should complete 10DLC brand and campaign registration before any SMS is sent. Sample messages should include opt-out language. Sending should be blocked when the campaign use case does not match the content, for example a 'customer care' campaign sending sales pitches.

findings.title: UK PECR and UK GDPR for B2B outreach: corporate addresses can be emailed with an opt-out, but sole traders need consent; PECR fines now reach £17.5m or 4%
findings.detail: The ICO's B2B guidance says PECR's consent rule for email and text does not apply to corporate subscribers (limited companies, LLPs and similar). The sender must still identify itself and give a valid opt-out, and the ICO says corporate opt-outs should be honoured. Sole traders and some partnerships count as individuals, so they need consent or the soft opt-in, and unclear cases should be treated as individuals. Live calls must be screened against TPS, CTPS and the sender's own do-not-call list. UK GDPR still applies to named business contacts. That means a legitimate-interests assessment, privacy information within one month when data comes from elsewhere, and an absolute right to object to direct marketing. Law firms report that the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 provisions commenced on 5 Feb 2026 (SI 2026/82). They raised the PECR maximum from £500k to £17.5m or 4% of global turnover and removed the 'seriousness' threshold. The ICO says its B2B guidance is under review because of the DUAA.
findings.why_it_matters: UK lead records need a subscriber-type field (corporate, sole trader or partnership, unknown). Sole traders and unknowns should be blocked from cold email unless consent or soft opt-in is recorded. TPS/CTPS screening is needed before calls. The first message should carry a privacy notice saying where the data came from. A stored LIA template per campaign and suppression lists kept indefinitely are also required.

findings.title: EU B2B cold email depends on the country: Germany requires prior consent even for B2B; France allows role-relevant B2B email with an opt-out; CNIL now requires consent for email tracking pixels
findings.detail: Germany's UWG §7(2) Nr. 2 treats email advertising without the addressee's prior express consent as an unreasonable nuisance in every case, with no consumer/business distinction. The only exception is §7(3) for existing customers buying similar products, with an opt-out notice at collection and in every message. Phone ads to businesses need at least presumed consent. In France, CNIL doctrine since 2005 allows email to a named professional address without consent if the message relates to the person's role and includes information and an easy opt-out. Elsewhere in the EU, GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) legitimate interests with a documented balancing test is the usual basis, under national ePrivacy rules. The CNIL's final recommendation on email tracking pixels (14 Apr 2026) requires prior consent for open-tracking pixels, with narrow exceptions, and a 14 Jul 2026 transition deadline for existing lists. Treating silence as consent is not allowed.
findings.why_it_matters: Outreach rules should be driven by country. Cold email to German recipients should be blocked by default unless consent is recorded. French cold email should be limited to role-relevant offers. Open-tracking pixels should be off by default for EU/EEA recipients, with click-based metrics used instead. Each EU campaign should store a legitimate-interests assessment.

findings.title: FTC Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule (16 CFR 465) in force since 21 Oct 2024; first public enforcement was warning letters on 22 Dec 2025
findings.detail: The rule permits civil penalties for several practices. These include fake reviews or testimonials, including AI-generated ones and those from people with no real experience. Also covered: reviews that misrepresent the reviewer's experience, incentives conditioned on positive or negative sentiment, undisclosed insider reviews from staff or family, company-controlled 'independent' review sites, review suppression, and knowingly buying or selling fake social-media indicators. On 22 Dec 2025 the FTC sent warning letters to 10 unnamed companies, flagging conduct such as paying employees to collect five-star reviews from friends and family. It cited penalties of up to $53,088 per violation. The FTC holds brands responsible for agents acting for them. A law-firm review in August 2026 reported no new formal 2026 cases.
findings.why_it_matters: Coaching programmes rely on student win posts and case studies. Operator AI should keep a testimonial vault with provenance for each item: a real verified person, a consent record, the date, any compensation or relationship disclosure, and typicality data. AI-generated or 'composite' testimonials should be blocked. The rule also bars review requests that reward only five-star reviews and any filtering that hides negative reviews.

findings.title: FTC proposal to bring business coaching under the Business Opportunity Rule (NPRM of 13 Jan 2025) is still unresolved; the existing rule is enforced against AI and income offers
findings.detail: On 13 Jan 2025 the FTC issued an NPRM to expand the Business Opportunity Rule (16 CFR 437) into a 'Business and Money-Making Opportunity Rule'. It would cover business coaching and investment offers that claim to help consumers build a business or earn income. Sellers would face bans on material misrepresentations and would need written substantiation for any earnings claim, provided on request. The proposal would not require the full disclosure document. A parallel MLM Earnings Claim Rule NPRM and ANPRM were also issued. Commissioners Ferguson, now Chair, and Holyoak voted no, and I found no evidence it has been finalised or withdrawn as of October 2026. Separately, the October 2021 Notices of Penalty Offenses on money-making opportunities went to more than 1,100 companies, including business coaching providers. They put those companies on notice that unsubstantiated profit and 'no experience needed' or 'risk-free' claims can bring civil penalties.
findings.why_it_matters: The safe design assumes coaching earnings claims are already regulated. Operator AI should store written substantiation for every income or results claim before it is published. Claims should be produced on request, and the 'growth operator' opportunity should not be described as risk-free or as needing no experience. Earnings claims should be versioned so they can be audited.

findings.title: 2026 FTC cases show what triggers action: Air AI (AI-agent business opportunity, 24 Mar 2026) and an MLM coach's lifestyle-based earnings claims (Apr 2026)
findings.detail: On 24 Mar 2026 the FTC filed a proposed order against Air AI, which sold 'conversational AI' access and licences, and its owners. The FTC alleged false earnings claims, false refund and buy-back guarantees, and missing Business Opportunity Rule disclosure documents and earnings statements, in violation of the Business Opportunity Rule and the Telemarketing Sales Rule. The order carries an $18M judgment, mostly suspended with $50k payable, and bans selling any business opportunity and making unsubstantiated earnings claims. In April 2026, a proposed order against MLM promoter Stormy Wellington treats images of homes, cars, purchases and travel as earnings representations. It requires written substantiation at the time a claim is made, available to anyone interested. Earlier coaching cases include Lurn, Automators AI and Ecommerce Empire Builders.
findings.why_it_matters: Operator AI's content approval gates should catch the patterns the FTC cites. That means flagging income and ROI claims, refund or guarantee language, and lifestyle imagery in ads, VSLs, webinar scripts and DM scripts, then routing them to the owner for substantiation and approval. Any 'done-for-you AI agent' or licence-resale offer should be checked against Business Opportunity Rule disclosure duties. Refund and guarantee terms should match what the sales team says.

findings.title: Click-to-Cancel: the 2024 rule was vacated (8th Cir., July 2025); the FTC restarted with an ANPRM (published 13 Mar 2026, comments closed 13 Apr 2026); ROSCA and state laws still apply
findings.detail: The Eighth Circuit vacated the FTC's amended Negative Option Rule in July 2025 on procedural grounds, because no preliminary regulatory analysis had been done. The FTC sent a draft ANPRM to OIRA on 30 Jan 2026, announced it on 11 Mar 2026, and published it on 13 Mar 2026, with comments due 13 Apr 2026. No new final rule exists. Sidley expects any new proposal to look like the 2024 version. The FTC keeps pursuing subscription cases (for example JustAnswer) under ROSCA and Section 5, and states and cities (for example New York City in April 2026) are adding their own click-to-cancel rules.
findings.why_it_matters: For recurring billing, such as the white-label SaaS seat, payment-plan programmes or continuity offers, Operator AI should collect express informed consent to recurring charges and show terms clearly before billing. Online cancellation should be as easy as sign-up. Each tenant should keep consent and cancellation logs.

findings.title: EU AI Act Article 50: chatbot disclosure and deepfake labelling have applied since 2 Aug 2026; generative AI already on the market has until 2 Dec 2026 for machine-readable marking
findings.detail: Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 applies from 2 August 2026. Under Art. 50(1), providers must design AI systems that interact with people so those people know they are dealing with AI, unless it is obvious. Under Art. 50(2), providers of generative systems must mark synthetic audio, image, video and text in a machine-readable, detectable way. Under Art. 50(4), deployers must disclose deepfakes, and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless a human has editorially reviewed it and taken responsibility. Disclosure must be clear and given at the latest at first interaction. The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, was published in the Official Journal on 24 Jul 2026 and in force from 27 Jul 2026. It did not defer Art. 50(1) or 50(4). It gave generative systems placed on the market before 2 Aug 2026 until 2 Dec 2026 for Art. 50(2) marking. Fines run up to €15M or 3% of worldwide turnover.
findings.why_it_matters: For EU leads and audiences, every AI-run DM, chat, email-reply agent and voice agent needs an AI-interaction disclosure at the first message. AI avatars, voice clones and face swaps in ads, VSLs and webinars need visible deepfake labels. Generated media should carry machine-readable marking (metadata or watermark) by 2 Dec 2026 at the latest. Logging human editorial review of AI-written public content supports the 50(4) exemption.

findings.title: EU Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content (final, 10 June 2026): multi-layer marking for providers and EU icons for deployers
findings.detail: The Commission published the final voluntary Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content on 10 June 2026 (press release IP/26/1328). It is meant to help providers and deployers comply with Article 50. Per secondary reports, the provider section commits signatories to machine-readable marking, with at least two layers where needed (for example metadata plus watermark). The deployer section includes an EU icon set for labelling AI-generated or AI-modified content. Once the Commission and AI Board find the Code adequate, signatories can rely on it to show compliance. Commission guidelines on Article 50's scope were also planned. Publication-date reports vary between 10 and 24 June.
findings.why_it_matters: The Code is a ready-made benchmark for Operator AI's provenance stack. Generated creatives should keep or add C2PA-style metadata plus a watermark, never strip upstream marks on export, and offer the EU label icons in the ad and creative builder for EU-facing content.

findings.title: EU AI Act high-risk duties for education and employment AI moved to 2 Dec 2027
findings.detail: The Digital Omnibus (Reg. (EU) 2026/1744) moved obligations for stand-alone high-risk systems in Annex III from 2 Aug 2026 to 2 Dec 2027. Annex III covers, among others, education (admission and evaluating learning outcomes) and employment (recruiting, selecting and evaluating workers). Product-embedded Annex I systems move to 2 Aug 2028. The Omnibus also adds a ban on AI generating non-consensual intimate imagery and CSAM, from 2 Dec 2026.
findings.why_it_matters: If Operator AI ranks or admits students, grades their competence for certification, or screens and scores setters and closers for hiring in the EU, those features may be high-risk from December 2027. That would bring risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight and transparency duties. Keeping such scoring advisory, with a human decision-maker and an audit log, preserves options.

findings.title: US state bot-disclosure laws: Maine (in force 23 Sept 2025) and Utah (narrowed 2025) require telling consumers they are talking to AI in sales conversations
findings.detail: Maine's 10 M.R.S. §1500-DD (P.L. 2025 c. 294, reported effective 23 Sept 2025) bars using an AI chatbot or other technology in trade with a consumer in a way that could lead a reasonable consumer to think they are dealing with a human, unless they get clear and conspicuous notice. A violation counts as a breach of the Maine Unfair Trade Practices Act. Utah's AI Policy Act, as amended by SB 226 (2025) and extended to July 2027 by SB 332, requires disclosure in two cases. One is when a consumer clearly and unambiguously asks whether they are talking to AI. The other is proactively in 'high-risk' interactions, meaning collection of sensitive data or personalised recommendations relied on for significant decisions. Utah offers a safe harbour for clear disclosure at the start and during the interaction. Meta's own docs flag California's bot-disclosure law (from memory: B&P Code §17940 et seq., 2019, not re-checked this session) as one that requires disclosure.
findings.why_it_matters: Operator AI should disclose AI by default at the start of every AI-run conversation in the US, not only in particular states. The agent should always answer 'are you a bot?' truthfully, and any instruction to pose as a human setter should be blocked. This one default meets Maine, Utah, California, Meta and EU Art. 50(1).

findings.title: New York requires a label on ads using AI 'synthetic performers' (GBL §396-b, effective 9 June 2026)
findings.detail: New York's S.8420-A/A.8887-B, codified at General Business Law §396-b, took effect on 9 June 2026. Anyone who produces or creates an ad that includes a 'synthetic performer' must conspicuously disclose it if the ad reaches New York audiences, including from out-of-state advertisers. A synthetic performer is a digitally created human-like figure not based on an identifiable real person. Penalties are $1,000 for a first violation and $5,000 for later ones, with no private right of action reported. Audio-only ads, AI used only for translating or dubbing a human performer, and some expressive works are exempt. One firm reports platforms must remove or fix a flagged ad within 5 days.
findings.why_it_matters: When the ad or creative studio generates AI presenters or UGC-style avatars, it should tag the asset as containing a synthetic performer and add a visible disclosure for any campaign that can reach New York. Without geo-exclusion, applying the label to all US ads is simplest. Deepfakes of real people fall under publicity and consent rules instead.

findings.title: California AI Transparency Act (SB 942 as amended by AB 853) took effect 2 Aug 2026: latent provenance marks, detection tools, platform duties from 2027
findings.detail: AB 853, signed 13 Oct 2025, delayed SB 942 to 2 Aug 2026. Covered generative AI providers (more than 1M monthly users, publicly accessible in California) must now embed latent provenance disclosures in AI-generated image, video and audio, offer a free AI-detection tool, and give users an option to add a visible label. AB 853 adds duties for large online platforms and generative AI hosting platforms from 1 Jan 2027, and for capture-device makers from 2028. One guide puts penalties at $5,000 per violation per day. Thresholds differ between secondary sources.
findings.why_it_matters: Operator AI is probably not a covered provider itself, but it relies on upstream generative AI vendors that are. Its media pipeline should keep latent disclosures and C2PA manifests on resize and export and must not strip them. It should also be ready for platforms to read and display provenance from 2027.

findings.title: Voice and likeness cloning: Tennessee's ELVIS Act covers simulated voices and the tools that make them; the federal NO FAKES Act cleared Senate Judiciary on 18 June 2026
findings.detail: Tennessee's ELVIS Act (effective 1 July 2024) added voice to the state's statutory right of publicity. It covers both a person's real voice and simulations of it, reaches non-commercial deepfakes, and creates liability for distributing technology whose primary purpose is producing someone's voice or likeness without authorisation. The rights extend to estates. Federally, the NO FAKES Act was reintroduced on 20 May 2026 (S.4591 / H.R.8915) and advanced by the Senate Judiciary Committee by unanimous voice vote on 18 June 2026. It would create a federal digital-replica right with DMCA-style notice and counter-notice, and would preempt most state digital-replica laws, apart from carve-outs for some existing state causes of action. It has not passed the full Senate as of the latest sources.
findings.why_it_matters: Voice-clone and avatar features for creator clients, such as AI webinar hosts, cloned-voice DMs or voice-note setters, need a signed digital-replica consent from the person cloned. It should set scope, channels, term and revocation, and be stored and checked before each generation. Cloning third parties such as celebrities or competitors should be blocked, and the system should be ready to act on takedown notices.

findings.title: Call recording and AI notetakers: about 11 all-party-consent states, CIPA class actions against AI notetakers, and no business-purpose exemption coming from California's SB 690
findings.detail: Secondary 2026 guides count 11 all-party-consent states: CA, DE, FL, IL, MD, MA, MT, NV, NH, PA and WA. For interstate calls they advise following the stricter state's rule. In re Otter.AI Privacy Litigation (N.D. Cal., No. 5:25-cv-06911) consolidates four 2025 class suits under ECPA, CIPA, BIPA and the CFAA. The theory is that a notetaker vendor that can use call data for its own purposes is an unconsented third-party eavesdropper. Customers may face vicarious exposure, CIPA allows $5,000 per violation, and similar suits target Fireflies (BIPA, December 2025) and others. The July 2026 amendment to California SB 690 dropped the proposed 'commercial business purpose' exemption from CIPA. It now only limits private pen-register suits over websites and apps, so there is no general business-purpose defence for recording.
findings.why_it_matters: For closer and coach calls, Operator AI should have the recorder or notetaker announce itself and get affirmative consent from every party, defaulting to all-party consent everywhere. Proof of consent should be stored with the recording. Vendor contracts and settings should stop recording vendors from training on or reusing call data. Biometric voiceprints should not be captured without BIPA-style written consent.

findings.title: US federal pressure on state AI laws: a Dec 2025 executive order and DOJ task force, while Colorado replaced its AI Act with a narrower law effective 1 Jan 2027
findings.detail: An executive order signed on 11 Dec 2025 ('Ensuring a National Policy Framework for AI') directed DOJ to challenge state AI laws and Commerce to list 'onerous' ones within 90 days. It also tied some BEAD broadband funding to those findings. The AI Litigation Task Force was reportedly set up on 9–10 Jan 2026. Child-safety laws are carved out, and state laws stay enforceable unless courts or Congress preempt them. Colorado's SB 26-189, signed 14 May 2026, repealed and replaced the 2024 Colorado AI Act. The new law is a narrower framework on automated decision-making, effective 1 Jan 2027, with AG enforcement and rulemaking only. DOJ has moved to intervene in xAI's challenge to the Colorado law.
findings.why_it_matters: State AI disclosure and ADMT rules may change or be enjoined, so compliance logic should live in a per-jurisdiction rules config, not in code. Until a court says otherwise, the strictest current state requirement should be treated as binding.
